newsitem.title: TAIWAN: E.Asia bullish on USDA soy, bearish on corn/wheat.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia bullish on USDA soy, bearish on corn/wheat.

text.p: Taiwanese buyers may soon enter the market for large quantities of soybeans after Wednesday's USDA crop report and South Korea is eyeing Argentine corn, but the Japanese are holding back, traders said on Thursday.

Traders in Taiwan said they had turned bullish on soybeans but bearish on corn and wheat after the USDA survey. They said the latest forecast for low U.S. soybean ending stocks had increased fears of potential crop damage from any early frost.
"The delayed (U.S.) soybean planting this year could put crops in danger of frost," a buyer at Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Corp said.
Taiwanese analysts said if frost damaged a significant part of the U.S. crop, soybean prices could top US$9.00 a bushel by April next year.

On Wednesday, Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) soybean futures closed mostly lower on a sharp fall in wheat and lower corn futures on the USDA report. The new crop November contract closed down, but held just above key support at $8.00 a bushel. "Current soybean prices already reflect most of the worries, but
the price will top nine dollars (a bushel) if the crop damage materialises," one analyst said.
Traders said Taiwan still needed more than 150,000 tonnes of soybean for its fourth quarter requirements and the bullish price forecasts could encourage buyers to place tenders soon.
But they said the USDA report was bearish news for the corn and wheat markets and the downward trend in U.S. futures seen overnight on Wednesday could accelerate and test support.
"Corn and wheat futures will have to find new price support after the improved ending stock and good supply data," one Taiwanese trader said.
In South Korea, traders said buyers were now expected to enter the market by Friday or early next week for between 250,000 tonnes to 300,000 tonnes of Argentine corn.
"We heard several feed companies would buy Argentine corn by this weekend because of the bearish outlook of the USDA crop report on Wednesday," a Seoul-based Japanese trader said.
Argentine corn is currently quoted at $158 a tonne C&F South Korea, about $5.00 to $10 a tonne below U.S. corn prices..
Traders said the Korea Feed Association could buy two or three cargoes of corn for February and March delivery.
But they said the predicted further falls in corn prices could be limited by the lagging maturity of the U.S. crop and the forecasts for cold weather in the Midwest.
Japanese grain buyers welcomed the USDA report, but said they were still wary of calling an end to the historically tight world grain supply/demand picture seen earlier this year.
"We were relieved at the new figures, since the unusually tight supply/demand will be eased," one senior trader said.
"We had already been forced to buy U.S. corn at a quicker pace than usual this year and had already covered up to 60 percent of our January to March requirements," he added.

Japanese buyers said they were now under less pressure to buy corn and wheat and that they could afford to wait for more plentiful supplies now predicted after the U.S. harvest and for a forecast further easing in trans-Pacific freight rates.
But traders said they still expected some shipment delays for U.S. grain later this year.
"The tight supply/demand will not change in one night. We still expect some delays for September and October shipments," another trader said.
The Agriculture Ministry announced on August 30 it would release up to 400,000 tonnes of corn from national feed grain stocks in the September/November period of this year.

"We're not going to review the release plan despite the USDA's new forecast. The supply concern is unchanged, and we can't lower our guard recklessly," said Mitsuhiro Yokoyama of the ministry's Livestock Industry Bureau.
Little change was also expected in the pace of Japan's oilseeds imports with nearly 30 percent of U.S. soybean equirements for November shipment, now covered, traders said.

They said the USDA figures were broadly within their forecasts and they were waiting for a distinct U.S. price trend to emerge and for the conclusion of delayed talks over local soymeal prices between soybean crushers and feed makers.

"We're negotiating soymeal prices with feed makers, and can't yet reach a conclusion," Masahiko Ozawa, assistant manager of Nisshin Oil Mills Ltd, said. "Unless the soymeal prices are agreed, we can't accelerate soybean imports," he said.
Japan's Food Agency said it welcomed estimate the USDA's figures which showed that U.S. wheat stock levels are rising.
"Stable supply and prices are our top priority. We welcome the USDA's new figures," a senior official at the agency said.
